comparison: Both evaluations support the claims about IL-25R-/- mice maintaining normal adaptive immunity while having defective innate responses (C4, C34-C44, C100-C102, C129). OpenEval emphasizes the comprehensive experimental evidence separating adaptive from innate defects, while peer reviewers found the findings interesting and accepted the basic phenotype without challenge.

Perfect agreement on chimera data (C51-C53, C108). Both evaluations support that IL-25R on hematopoietic cells is necessary and sufficient for parasite clearance. OpenEval notes the appropriate experimental design with proper controls, while peer reviewers accepted the findings without criticism.

Perfect agreement on IL-25 and IL-4 synergy claims (C6, C54-C57). Both evaluations support the synergy data from Figure 3B-C. OpenEval emphasizes the quantitative evidence and statistical significance, while peer reviewers acknowledged the synergy as part of core findings without challenge.

Major disagreement on ILC dispensability (C7, C63-C65, C110-C112, C132). OpenEval finds the data strongly supportive that ILCs are not required for protective immunity, while peer reviewers rated this UNCERTAIN, raising substantial concerns about the definitiveness of anti-CD90 depletion approach, noting issues with tissue location and inflammatory ILC2 phenotype.

Both evaluations support the temporal data showing late IL-25 effectiveness (C5, C66-C72). OpenEval emphasizes the statistical analysis and interpretation that IL-25 acts on effector mechanisms rather than adaptive immunity. Peer reviewers acknowledged the timing experiments and noted correlation with ILC2 upregulation, though they questioned whether ILC2s were the critical effectors.

Perfect agreement on innate cell activation data (C82-C86, C119). Both evaluations support the flow cytometry findings showing IL-25 effects on macrophages and eosinophils. OpenEval notes the comprehensive nature of the data with appropriate quantification, while peer reviewers accepted these findings without raising concerns.

Perfect agreement on in vitro synergy data (C87-C89, C125). Both evaluations support the bone marrow-derived macrophage experiments demonstrating IL-25 and IL-4 synergy. OpenEval emphasizes the appropriate experimental design testing all combinations, while peer reviewers implicitly accepted these findings as part of the overall synergy demonstration.

Perfect agreement on IL-4Rα dependency (C91-C95, C126). Both evaluations support the genetic evidence from Il4ra-/- mice showing complete loss of IL-25 effects. OpenEval notes the strong support from both functional and cellular readouts, while peer reviewers accepted these findings without concerns.

Partial disagreement on overarching conclusions (C8, C99, C130, C133). OpenEval finds the integrated conclusion well-supported by converging evidence from multiple experimental systems. Peer reviewers rated this UNCERTAIN, considering conclusions 'may be premature' specifically regarding ILC independence, requesting additional experiments or revision of major conclusions.

Both address ILC2 response data (C73-C75), though with different emphasis. OpenEval notes the quantitative observations are supported but questions functional significance given ILC depletion results. Peer reviewers noted Figure 4H shows IL-25 upregulating ILC2 correlating with protection, but questioned whether ILC2s were critical effectors.

Overlap on macrophage-related mechanistic claims (C120-C122, C124). OpenEval supports the overall conclusion about IL-25's role in macrophage activation while noting C122 is more speculative. Peer reviewers' UNCERTAIN rating for the broader conclusions reflects concerns about whether effects are ILC2-mediated versus direct innate cell effects.
